headline: High risk of prompt injection and data leakage via shared MCP/networked workflows; capability conflicts and cascading errors are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can use direct function calls or an MCP server, and haystack explicitly uses MCP servers. That shared bridge makes prompt injection plausible if aci ingests haystack outputs or shared files as instructions. The pair lacks provenance controls in the profiles, but the interaction is not directly documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF aci consumes haystack-generated text from an MCP channel as instructions
IF both agents are connected to the same MCP server without provenance tagging
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following on MCP-fed text
Add provenance labels to all MCP messages
Restrict aci to allowlisted MCP tools only
Insert a human review step before executing MCP-derived actions
requires-engineering: isolate the agents onto separate MCP servers

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches CRM, email, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress; haystack also has broad egress and can call MCP servers. Even though haystack's touched data class is limited, the pair can move sensitive aci data through networked retrieval or logging paths, so leakage is plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF aci forwards CRM or email content into haystack queries or logs
IF haystack relays retrieved content to external REST/MCP endpoints
mitigations: Disable sending raw CRM/email fields to haystack
Redact sensitive fields before retrieval
Turn off verbose request/response logging
Use separate credentials for each agent
requires-engineering: enforce workspace and network isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, and aci supports multiple instances while haystack can use MCP servers. That creates overlapping mutable network/API activity and possible race conditions on shared external resources, though the profiles do not prove shared write targets. Uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same CRM, sheet, or REST-backed record set
IF no external locking or idempotency keys are used
mitigations: Assign disjoint API credentials
Add idempotency keys to writes
Serialize writes through one orchestrator
Check for duplicate updates before commit
requires-engineering: add resource-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: haystack is a search-RAG agent and can consume upstream text, while aci can generate CRM/email/calendar actions. If haystack treats aci output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF haystack uses aci output as retrieved truth without verification
IF haystack triggers downstream actions based on aci-produced summaries
mitigations: Require source citations before actioning outputs
Add a verification step against primary data
Limit haystack to read-only summarization
Log and review action-triggering prompts
requires-engineering: separate retrieval from execution

E_compliance.rationale: aci touches email, CRM, calendar, customer support, and secrets management, while haystack is documented only as touching anonymous usage statistics. The profiles do not show residency or retention controls, but aci's data classes make compliance mismatch plausible if those records flow into haystack's networked processing. I cite both because the risk is pairwise.
conditions: IF regulated customer or email data is sent from aci into haystack processing
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of haystack inputs
Document retention for both systems
Minimize logged payloads
Review data-processing agreements
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
